Academic Calendar Committee (ACC), Chair Donnelly - Informational Report regarding merger of the Academic and the Accelerated Online Calendars - Chair Donnelly offered her committee’s conceptual report, noting that formal UM amendments for action would be forthcoming.
She explained that the accelerated online programs do not currently fall under the umbrella of the semester-based academic calendar.
This presents various problems for students, including the fact that financial aid restrictions prevent students from concurrently taking classes from both calendars.
The proposed ‘calendar merger’ would give students greater flexibility.
If approved, such a calendar merger would be operationally complex to implement as changes would need to be enacted not only to the University Manual, but within eCampus and the financial aid and billing systems as well.
Faculty members are expected to be impacted by the change and the committee would like to hear from faculty about their concerns as the relevant amendments are being drafted.

In general terms, the fall and summer session start dates would generally not be affected but the spring semester online classes would start later in the month than is currently the case.
The informational report was accepted. c.

Presentation - Catalog Descriptions Standardization Project - Certificates Demonstration Special Guests: Indrani Mandal and Liam McKenzie from the URI Lab, along with Faculty Senate Specialist Genvieve Spitale, provided an overview of the initiative to standardize descriptions to make for a more user-friendly database, as well as improve the readability and searchability of the catalog.
The project will have the added benefit of greatly reducing the amount of staff time spent manually correcting new proposals in Kuali.
The ultimate goal is to expand the initiative to all programs and specializations, but this initial attempt has focused on Certificates as a sort of pilot project to test the programming.
A summary of the need and rationale for this project was provided.
It was noted that the need for a ‘program description template’ has been called for by Enrollment Services for a long time, as there is considerable variability in the way that descriptions are written, which has implications not only for consistency of appearance, but also for coding in Ecampus.

The guests explained that the AI Lab will run an Auto Check (analogous to ‘spell-check’) on new draft proposals to look for missing data fields, typos, formatting problems, etc. and alert proposers of the need to make corrections before formally submitting their proposals.
The Lab generates an email with suggestions, but it will be up to the proposers to make the changes; the AI will not make corrections independently.
Details of the methodology were discussed in some detail (programming language, turn-around times, privacy and transparency considerations, as well as any academic freedom implications for faculty members).
FSEC also discussed implementation of the model and the best way to get the word out to faculty.
Faculty will need to be advised ahead of time that their proposals will initially be assessed by the AI Lab, before being processed through the normal curricular approval channels.
Ideally, a training would be run for faculty members, but at a minimum, clear instructions will need to be provided.
